title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Purpose
-------
This page codifies Redwood Inference SRE standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. The goal is to ensure predictable availability and latency for customer-facing inference services while controlling cost and providing clear procedures for incident handling and post-incident learning.

Audience
--------
SRE, platform, serving-runtime, product, and on-call engineers. Managers and cross-functional partners should reference the Ownership and Escalation section.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets
-------------------------
Summary: Every customer-facing service must have at least one SLO aligned to customer experience (availability or latency) and one operational SLO (latency or queueing) where appropriate. SLO windows are 30-day rolling by default. Error budgets are tracked monthly and drive rollouts and feature releases.

SLO guide:
- Define a primary SLO that maps to customer experience (e.g., inference request success rate or p99 tail latency for small requests).
- Use secondary SLOs for performance dimensions (p95/p99 latency, cold-start frequency, queue wait time).
- Default SLO window: 30-day rolling. For enterprise contracts consider 90-day windows in coordination with Sales/Legal.
- Error budget policy: Burn rate tracked continuously. When burn rate exceeds thresholds, trigger progressive mitigation and release freezes.

Canonical SLO table (examples):

Service | SLI | Target | Window | Error budget
-------|-----|--------|--------|------------
Serving API | Successful request rate (2xx / total) | 99.95% availability | 30d rolling | 0.05% monthly (~21.6 mins of downtime)
Realtime chat (small payload) | p95 response latency | <= 150ms | 30d rolling | latency budget for p95 deviations
Embeddings service | p99 latency | <= 500ms | 30d rolling | latency budget for p99 deviations
Batch jobs | Job success rate | 99.9% per run | 30d rolling | budgeted retries and backoff windows

SLI definition rules:
- Measurement point: ingress proxy (edge) and primary backend for cross-checks. Record both client-observed and server-observed SLIs.
- Exclude scheduled maintenance (with calendar entries) from SLO windows.
- Clearly document what constitutes a failed request (5xx, timeouts, model OOM, truncated response).

Error budget burn policy:
- Burn rate < 1x: normal operations.
- Burn rate 1x-4x sustained for 1 hour: Notify owners, create a mitigation plan, restrict large rollouts.
- Burn rate 4x-8x sustained for 30 minutes: Pause non-critical deployments, scale capacity if safe, prioritize fixes.
- Burn rate > 8x: Escalate to SRE manager and director, consider incident declaration.

2) Capacity Planning
---------------------
Objectives: Ensure headroom to meet SLOs under expected traffic and during planned growth. Capacity planning includes GPU pool sizing, autoscaling policies, cold-start budgets, and network/storage IO provisioning.

Process (quarterly):
1. Traffic and usage forecasting: product + metrics team provide 12-week and 52-week forecasts (traffic per route, payload size distribution, expected latency percentile targets).
2. Demand modeling: simulate traffic against service performance curves (p50/p95/p99 latency vs tokens/sec).
3. Headroom targets: maintain minimum 25% spare serving capacity for hosted API; Dedicated customers have contract-specific headroom agreed in their SLOs.
4. Procurement / reservation plan: request additional GPU reservations or cloud credits 8-12 weeks ahead of expected demand increases.
5. Review autoscaling policies: verify scale-up time <= expected traffic ramp window, set cooldowns to avoid oscillation.

Capacity planning checklist:
- Owner: eng-sre capacity planning subteam.
- Inputs: historical QPS, model size mix, sequence length distribution, current KV cache hit rates.
- Outputs: fleet sizing sheet (GPU count by type), autoscaler configs, pre-warming plans, and cost estimate.

3) Reliability Initiatives
-------------------------
Purpose: Structured program for proactive reliability work (reducing p99 latency, increasing cache hit rates, improving graceful degradation). Each initiative follows a charter and measurable success criteria.

Initiative charter template:
- Title
- Owner
- Motivation and hypothesis
- Success metrics (SLO impact, cost delta)
- Timeline and milestones
- Rollout and rollback plan

Examples of recurring initiatives:
- Prefix/KV cache coverage increase (goal: +15% hit rate within 3 months).
- Automatic fallback to quantized model variant under load (goal: reduce p99 latency spikes by 30%).
- Continuous batching improvements to reduce per-token CPU cost by 10%.

4) Incident Review Standards
---------------------------
Post-incident reviews (PIRs) are mandatory for incidents that meet severity thresholds (SEV2/SEV1) or that consume >25% of the monthly error budget for any SLO.

PIR requirements:
- Timeline: publish preliminary incident notes within 48 hours and a full PIR within 14 days.
- Content: incident summary, timeline of events, detection and mitigation actions, root cause analysis (RCA), impact quantification (customers, error budget, cost), and a prioritized action list with owners and due dates.
- Severity mapping: define SEV1 (customer-impacting >50% customers or global failure), SEV2 (subset customers or degraded latency), SEV3 (minor or internal).
- Blameless culture: focus on system fixes and process changes. Include mitigations to prevent recurrence and a verification plan.

PIR template checklist:
1. Executive summary (1-2 paragraphs)
2. Affected services and SLOs
3. Detection timeline (timestamps, signals)
4. Mitigation actions and sequencing
5. Root cause(s) and contributing factors
6. Action items with owners and due dates
7. Postmortem review meeting notes and sign-off

5) Operational Tooling and Alerts
--------------------------------
Monitoring and alerting standards:
- SLO-driven alerts only: prioritize alerts that indicate SLO degradation. Avoid noisy infra-only alerts that do not correlate to customer impact.
- Burn-rate alerts: critical. Configure multi-level burn-rate alerts (1h, 6h, 24h windows) and integrate with on-call runbook links.
- Paging policy: only alert on-call when thresholds indicate imminent or ongoing SLO violation. Non-paging notifications route to owners for low-urgency issues.

Required observability dashboards and tooling:
- SLO dashboard per service (availability, latency percentiles, error budget remaining)
- On-call playbook links on dashboard panels
- Tracing and flamegraphs for p99 investigations (sample rate >= 5% for heavy tails)
- Cost and token usage dashboard tied to model variants
- Canary and rollout dashboards for new model versions

Recommended alerts and thresholds (examples):
- SLO burn rate > 2x sustained for 30m: pager to primary on-call
- p99 latency > target for 10% of requests in 15m window: notify owners
- Node OOM / GPU OOM: non-paging alert to infra on-call unless correlated to SLO loss
- Autoscaler failure to scale within expected window: pager to infra on-call

6) SRE Runbooks (canonical patterns)
-----------------------------------
All runbooks must be concise, actionable, and linked to monitoring panels. Each runbook header should include: owner, severity level, detection signal, immediate mitigation steps, escalation path, and verification steps.

Canonical runbook: "Serving API high error rate"
- Owner: serving-runtime team (on-call rota)
- Signal: 5xx rate > 0.5% and SLO burn rate > 1x for 15m
- Immediate steps (0-15m):
  1. Acknowledge page and set incident channel (Slack#sre-incidents).
  2. Check dashboard: error budget, p95/p99 latency, and recent deploys.
  3. If new deploy in last 30 minutes: rollback to previous stable tag and observe.
  4. Identify if errors are load-related (CPU/GPU saturation) or code-related (stack traces, exception patterns).
  5. If saturation, scale up capacity or enable burst pool. If code-related, apply hotfix or rollback.
- Escalation: if unresolved in 30 minutes escalate to service owner and SRE manager.
- Post-incident: create PIR if SEV2+ or if >25% monthly error budget used.

Canonical runbook: "High p99 latency on Realtime Chat"
- Signal: p99 latency exceeds target by >25% for 10m
- Steps: check KV cache hit rate, model variant fallbacks, queue depth, and GPU utilization. Temporarily route traffic to lower latency variant or increase dedicated capacity for critical customers.

Runbook quality checklist:
- Steps numbered, with commands and links to dashboards and logs
- Include safe rollback commands and traffic-routing snippet (kubectl / routing CLI examples)
- Expected verification steps and criteria to close incident

7) Ownership and Escalation
---------------------------
- SLO owner: service product or platform owner (documented in service metadata).
- On-call owner: team-level rotas with primary and secondary.
- Escalation ladder: primary on-call -> service owner -> SRE manager -> Eng director.
- Release policy: if error budget is exhausted for a service, all non-critical releases must be paused until error budget is replenished or a mitigation plan is approved by the SRE manager.

Appendix: Example commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Check SLO burn rate (CLI):
  redwood-observability slo burn-rate --service serving-api --window 1h
- Rollback deploy (example kubectl):
  kubectl -n serving rollout undo deployment/serving-api --to-revision=42
- Temporarily route traffic to fallback model variant (routing CLI example):
  redwood-route set --service=chat --variant=quantized-v1 --weight=100

References and Related Docs
--------------------------
- eng-sre: capacity planning templates and historical fleet sheets (linked in related_pages)
- eng-serving-runtime: runtime-architecture and kernel scheduling docs for perf guidance

Document maintenance
--------------------
- Owner: eng-sre (capacity & reliability subteam)
- Review cadence: annual review and after any SEV1/SEV2 PIR.
- Change process: propose changes via PR in the confluence-docs repo and request reviewer approval from SRE leads.

This document is intended to be the canonical reference for SRE practices at Redwood Inference. For questions or clarifications, contact the eng-sre mailing list or the document owner.
